chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, he said:
I asked him about the beetle that falls into the water: may wudu (ablution) be performed from it? He said: Yes, there is no harm in it. I said: Then what about the scorpion? He said: Pour it out.

So the proper way regarding this report, in what relates to the command to pour out that in which the scorpion has fallen, is that we carry it upon recommendation rather than prohibition and obligation.

key_terms.أَرِقْهُ: pour it out; instruction concerning the water
key_terms.أَيُتَوَضَّأُ: may wudu (ablution) be performed; asking about ritual use of the water
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: recommendation; the interpretive basis for understanding the command
key_terms.الْإِيجَابِ: obligation; negated here as the intended force of the command
key_terms.الْخُنْفَسَاءِ: the beetle; an insect discussed here in relation to water purity
key_terms.الْعَقْرَبُ: the scorpion; the second creature mentioned in the ruling
key_terms.الْمَاءِ: water; the substance whose ritual usability is being assessed
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm in it; indicating permissibility

ai.seo_question: Can wudu (ablution) be performed with water into which a beetle or scorpion has fallen?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling on water into which certain creatures have fallen. It indicates that water remains usable for wudu (ablution) when a beetle falls into it, while the instruction regarding a scorpion is understood as a recommendation to discard the water, not as an obligatory prohibition.
